title: A Meta-Analysis of Signaling Principle in Multimedia Learning Environments https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11423-020-09748-7
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page summarises Alpizar, Adesope, and Wong's meta-analysis of 44 effect sizes across 29 studies on 'signaling' -- cues such as arrows, highlighting, or colour coding that direct learner attention within multimedia materials. The overall finding is that signaling reliably benefits learning, though the size of the benefit depends on study quality, participant characteristics like prior knowledge and grade level, and presentation features such as pacing, media type, and the presence of images. Dynamic signals (changing over time, as in animations) outperformed static ones, and signaling was particularly beneficial for students with low prior knowledge who are struggling to grasp new material. Learner-paced presentations beat system-paced ones, and -- consistent with Barton's other multimedia-learning pages -- presentations without extraneous images sometimes outperformed those with images, since irrelevant images can distract. Shorter treatments (under three minutes) and shorter overall study completion times (under an hour) also tended to be more effective. Barton frames this as strong, generalisable evidence that teachers should feel free to experiment with different signaling techniques across their materials.
points: Signaling -- cues like arrows, highlighting, or colour that direct attention in multimedia materials -- reliably benefits learning across 29 studies and 44 effect sizes.
Dynamic signals (changing over time, as in animation) outperform static ones, and the benefit is strongest for students with low prior knowledge.
Learner-paced presentations outperform system-paced ones, and images that are not directly relevant can distract rather than help.
Shorter treatments (under three minutes) and shorter overall study sessions (under an hour) tended to show stronger effects than longer ones.
quotes: The current meta-analysis indicates that presentations with signaling have benefits for learning. Results from this meta-analysis can guide educators and instructional designers in their effective use of signaling techniques to facilitate optimal learning outcomes, especially in complex multimedia environments

Signals are beneficial for student learning, regardless of the type of signal used. This suggests that teachers should feel free to experiment with different types of signals to find what works best for their students and subject matter
Dynamic signals may be more effective than static signals. Dynamic signals are those that change over time, such as animations or videos
Signals are especially beneficial for students with low prior knowledge. Teachers should use signals to help students who are struggling to grasp new material
Learner-paced presentations are more effective than system-paced presentations
Presentations without images may be more effective than presentations with images. Images can be distracting to students, especially if they are not relevant to the lesson
